Why Ghanaian SMEs are slow to adopt AI tools

By Efua Asante · 14 March 2025

Small and medium-sized enterprises make up the large majority of registered businesses in Ghana, yet very few of them use artificial intelligence in their daily work. A new survey of 240 firms in Accra and Kumasi suggests the reasons are practical rather than cultural: owners say the tools are too expensive, too hard to set up, and too far from the problems they face every day.

The survey, carried out between June and September 2024, asked owner-managers about chatbots, automated bookkeeping, demand forecasting and image recognition. Only 18% of respondents said their firm used any AI-based tool at least once a week. Among firms with fewer than ten employees, the figure fell to 9%.

Cost comes first

When asked to name the single biggest obstacle, 41% of owners chose cost. Subscription prices are usually quoted in US dollars, and several respondents said that exchange-rate swings made monthly fees impossible to plan for. "We tried an accounting assistant for three months and the bill doubled when the cedi fell," said the owner of a printing business in Kumasi.

Skills were the second most common barrier, named by 27% of respondents. Many owners said they would need to hire or train someone before they could rely on an AI tool, and that training courses were mostly offered in Accra and in English only.

Infrastructure and trust

Unreliable electricity and mobile data costs were mentioned by 15% of respondents. A smaller group, about 9%, said they did not trust automated systems with customer data, especially after high-profile fraud cases involving mobile money.

Firms that had adopted AI tended to share three traits: they already kept digital records, at least one staff member had a tertiary qualification, and they sold to customers outside their home region. These firms reported faster invoicing and fewer stock-outs, although the survey could not establish whether AI caused the improvement.

What could change

The authors of the survey recommend pricing in local currency, short practical training delivered in local languages, and shared services through business associations so that small firms can split the cost of a single licence. They also call for a follow-up study in the agriculture sector, which was under-represented in the sample.
